questions.option_d: either the police or the thief
questions.explanation: We cannot tell whether the police or the thief had the clever plan.

questions.question_text: In "Smiling happily, the child ran to her mother," the phrase "Smiling happily" modifies —
questions.explanation: The child is the one smiling, matching the subject.

questions.question_text: In "the tall dark handsome stranger," the headword is —
questions.explanation: All three adjectives modify the noun 'stranger', which is the headword.

questions.question_text: In "a rather interesting old story about pirates," the headword is —
questions.explanation: 'Story' is the noun everything else describes; 'about pirates' post-modifies it.

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank with the correctly ordered adjectives: "She wore a ___ dress." (beautiful / long / red / silk)
questions.explanation: Adjective order: opinion (beautiful), size (long), colour (red), material (silk).

questions.question_text: Fill in the blank with the correctly ordered adjectives: "He bought a ___ table." (small / round / wooden)
questions.explanation: Adjective order: size (small), shape (round), material (wooden).

questions.question_text: "Having been delayed by traffic, the meeting started without me." The error is —
questions.explanation: 'Having been delayed' should describe a person, but the subject is 'the meeting'.

questions.question_text: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
questions.option_a: While walking home, I got wet.
questions.option_b: Walking home, the rain soaked my clothes.
questions.option_c: While I was walking home, it rained.
questions.option_d: I got wet while walking home.
questions.explanation: In (b) the rain cannot walk home; the modifier has no proper subject to attach to.

questions.question_text: "The thief stole a car from the showroom with tinted windows." The phrase "with tinted windows" should modify "car" but sits near "showroom." This is a —
questions.explanation: The modifier is too far from the word it should describe, so it attaches to the wrong noun.

questions.question_text: In "Children who play outside often are healthier," the word "often" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Often' sits between two verbs, so it is unclear whether it modifies 'play' or 'are'.

questions.question_text: "Running down the stairs, my bag fell open." The error is —
questions.explanation: The bag was not running down the stairs; the modifier needs a person as subject.

questions.question_text: "Exhausted from the journey, the bed felt wonderful." The error is —
questions.explanation: The bed was not exhausted; the modifier dangles without a matching subject.

questions.question_text: "Young and inexperienced, the task seemed difficult to him." The error is —
questions.explanation: 'Young and inexperienced' should describe a person, not 'the task'.

questions.question_text: In "sleeping pills," the word "sleeping" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Sleeping' tells the purpose of the pills (pills for sleeping), acting as a noun modifier.

questions.question_text: In "a crying baby," the word "crying" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Crying' describes what the baby is doing — a participle acting as an adjective.

questions.question_text: In "I have a letter to post," the phrase "to post" is a —
questions.explanation: The infinitive phrase follows the noun 'letter' and tells which letter.

questions.question_text: In "He is the right man to do the job," the phrase "to do the job" is a —
questions.explanation: It follows the noun 'man' and identifies which man.

questions.question_text: "My brother who lives in Dhaka is a doctor." (The speaker has more than one brother.) The clause "who lives in Dhaka" is a —
questions.explanation: The clause is essential to identify which brother, so it is restrictive (no commas).

questions.question_text: "Dhaka, which is the capital of Bangladesh, is crowded." The clause "which is the capital of Bangladesh" is a —
questions.explanation: Set off by commas, it adds extra information about an already identified noun.

questions.question_text: In "The reason why he left is unknown," the clause "why he left" is a —
questions.explanation: The relative adverb clause follows 'reason' and completes its meaning.

questions.question_text: In "The place where we met was beautiful," the clause "where we met" is a —
questions.explanation: The clause follows the noun 'place' and tells which place.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "After finishing the exam, the bell rang."
questions.option_a: After the exam finishing, the bell rang.
questions.option_b: After finishing the exam, we heard the bell.
questions.option_c: After finishing the exam, ringing was the bell.
questions.option_d: After finishing the exam, the bell was rung loudly.
questions.explanation: 'We' are the ones who finished the exam, so the subject must be 'we'.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "Being a rainy day, the match was postponed."
questions.option_a: The match was postponed being a rainy day.
questions.option_b: As it was a rainy day, the match was postponed.
questions.option_c: Being a rainy day, postponing the match happened.
questions.option_d: Being a rainy day, the match postponed itself.
questions.explanation: The participle needs a matching subject; rewriting with 'it was' removes the dangle.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "To make a cake, the oven must be hot."
questions.option_a: To make a cake, you must heat the oven.
questions.option_b: The oven must be hot to make a cake by it.
questions.option_c: To make a cake, the oven must be heated by heat.
questions.option_d: To make a cake, hot must be the oven.
questions.explanation: 'You' are the one making the cake, so 'you' must be the subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the sentence WITHOUT a dangling modifier.
questions.option_c: While eating, I heard the dog bark.
questions.option_d: While eating, the food tasted good.
questions.explanation: Only in (b) does 'I', the eater, serve as the subject of the main clause.

questions.question_text: In "those two little old red wooden houses," the number of pre-modifiers is —
questions.explanation: 'Those, two, little, old, red, wooden' — six words modify 'houses'.

questions.question_text: In "my first two attempts," the pre-modifiers are —
questions.explanation: All three words come before the headword 'attempts' and modify it.

questions.question_text: In "The movie was very interesting," the word "very" is —
questions.explanation: 'Very' strengthens the adjective 'interesting'; it does not modify 'movie' directly.

questions.question_text: In "I only told him the truth," the word "only" modifies —
questions.explanation: 'Only' sits before the verb, limiting the action: I did nothing else but tell.

questions.question_text: In "I told him only the truth," the word "only" modifies —
questions.explanation: 'Only' sits before 'the truth': I told him the truth and nothing else.

questions.question_text: In "The man standing there is my father," the phrase "standing there" is a —
questions.explanation: It is short for 'who is standing there' and follows the noun 'man'.

questions.question_text: In "The documents signed yesterday are on the desk," the phrase "signed yesterday" is a —
questions.explanation: Short for 'which were signed yesterday', it follows 'documents'.

questions.question_text: In "Anyone caught cheating will be punished," the phrase "caught cheating" is a —
questions.explanation: Short for 'who is caught cheating', it follows the pronoun 'anyone'.

questions.question_text: In "The girl in the red dress dancing gracefully is my cousin," the noun "girl" has —
questions.explanation: 'In the red dress' and 'dancing gracefully' both follow and describe 'girl'.

questions.question_text: In "A man of great courage saved the child," the phrase "of great courage" is a —
questions.explanation: The prepositional phrase follows 'man' and describes what kind of man.

questions.question_text: In "The news of his success spread fast," the phrase "of his success" is a —
questions.explanation: It follows the noun 'news' and tells which news.

questions.question_text: In "a bus driver," the word "bus" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Bus' is a noun modifying another noun, 'driver'.

questions.question_text: "Having completed the survey, the results were published." The error is —
questions.explanation: The results did not complete the survey; the modifier lacks a proper subject.

questions.question_text: "Being tired, the movie seemed boring to me." The error is —
questions.explanation: 'Being tired' should describe 'me', but the subject is 'the movie'.

questions.question_text: "Walking slowly, the street looked endless." The error is —
questions.explanation: The street was not walking; the participle phrase dangles.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence (set 3).
questions.option_a: Covered in mud, the car washed the boy.
questions.option_b: Covered in mud, the boy washed the car.
questions.option_c: Covered in mud, the car was washed by the boy.
questions.option_d: Covered in mud, washing was done.
questions.explanation: The boy is the one covered in mud, so 'the boy' must be the subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence (set 4).
questions.option_a: To improve your English, importance is vocabulary.
questions.option_b: To improve your English, you should build your vocabulary.
questions.option_c: To improve your English, vocabulary important is.
questions.option_d: To improve your English, vocabulary is important.
questions.explanation: 'You' are the one improving, so the subject must be 'you'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct sentence (set 5).
questions.option_a: While cooking, the baby was sleeping the kitchen.
questions.option_b: While I was cooking, the baby slept peacefully.
questions.option_c: While cooking, the baby slept peacefully.
questions.option_d: While cooking, sleeping was the baby.
questions.explanation: Only (b) gives the cooking a proper subject, 'I'.

questions.question_text: "The dog barked at the man with a loud voice." The phrase "with a loud voice" is —
questions.explanation: It may describe the dog or the man, so it must be moved next to the right noun.

questions.question_text: "He sold his car to a friend with four doors." The problem is —
questions.explanation: 'With four doors' should describe the car, not the friend.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "I met a girl at the party with green eyes."
questions.option_a: With green eyes, I met a girl at the party.
questions.option_b: I met a girl with green eyes at the party.
questions.option_c: I met at the party a girl with eyes green.
questions.option_d: I met a girl at the party with green.
questions.explanation: 'With green eyes' must sit next to 'girl', the noun it describes.

questions.question_text: "The manager praised the worker with a smile." The phrase "with a smile" is —
questions.explanation: We cannot tell whether the manager or the worker was smiling.

questions.question_text: "Flying over the city, the lights looked tiny." The error is —
questions.explanation: The lights were not flying; the modifier needs a person as subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "Hidden behind the curtain, the thief could not see the child."
questions.option_a: Hidden behind the curtain, the child was seen by the thief clearly.
questions.option_b: Hidden behind the curtain, the thief was unseen by seeing.
questions.option_c: Hidden behind the curtain, the child could not be seen by the thief.
questions.option_d: Hidden behind the curtain, seeing was impossible for the thief.
questions.explanation: The child is the one hidden, so 'the child' must be the subject.

questions.question_text: "Shocked by the news, tears filled her eyes." The error is —
questions.explanation: Tears cannot be shocked; the modifier needs 'she' as the subject.

questions.question_text: In "the recently built bridge," the word "recently" modifies —
questions.explanation: 'Recently' is an adverb modifying the participle 'built'.

questions.question_text: In "a well-known writer," the word "well" modifies —
questions.explanation: 'Well' is an adverb modifying the participle 'known'.

questions.question_text: In "the above statement," the word "above" is a —
questions.explanation: Here 'above' acts as an adjective before the noun 'statement'.

questions.question_text: In "The then president gave a speech," the word "then" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Then' means 'at that time' and modifies 'president' as an adjective.

questions.question_text: In "his timely arrival," the word "timely" is a —
questions.explanation: Despite ending in -ly, 'timely' is an adjective here, before the noun.

questions.question_text: In "A friendly smile greeted us," the word "friendly" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Friendly' is an adjective describing 'smile' before the noun.

questions.question_text: In "The lonely traveler walked on," the word "lonely" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Lonely' is an adjective placed before the noun 'traveler'.

questions.question_text: In "an early train," the word "early" is a —
questions.explanation: 'Early' is an adjective describing 'train' before the noun.

questions.question_text: "Looking through the window, the garden appeared lovely." The error is —
questions.explanation: The garden was not looking through the window; the modifier dangles.

questions.question_text: In "The garden looks beautiful," the word "beautiful" is —
questions.option_c: a subject complement, not a modifier
questions.explanation: 'Beautiful' completes the linking verb 'looks' and describes the subject; it modifies nothing.

questions.question_text: In "She seems happy today," the word "happy" is —
questions.explanation: After the linking verb 'seems', 'happy' describes 'she' but is a complement, not a modifier.

questions.question_text: In "They elected him president," the word "president" is —
questions.explanation: 'President' completes the object 'him'; it does not modify a noun.

questions.question_text: "Winking at the audience, the magician's assistant disappeared." The error is —
questions.explanation: The assistant was not winking (the magician was), so the phrase attaches to the wrong subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "After being painted, the artist admired the portrait."
questions.option_a: After painting the portrait, the artist admired it.
questions.option_b: After the painting, the artist admired the portrait being.
questions.option_c: After being painted, the artist admired.
questions.option_d: After being painted, the artist was admired by the portrait.
questions.explanation: The portrait was painted, not the artist; the doer 'the artist' must match 'painting'.

questions.question_text: "Hoping for a promotion, the long hours seemed worthwhile to Karim." The error is —
questions.explanation: 'Hoping' should describe Karim, but the grammatical subject is 'the long hours'.

questions.question_text: "As a mother of five, the school run is exhausting." The error is —
questions.explanation: The school run is not a mother of five; the phrase needs a person as its subject.

questions.question_text: Which opening phrase is acceptable as a sentence modifier (disjunct)?
questions.explanation: Comment clauses like 'to be honest' are accepted disjuncts; the others dangle without a matching subject.

questions.question_text: "Generally speaking, the results were quite good." The phrase "Generally speaking" is —
questions.option_c: an accepted disjunct, not a dangling modifier
questions.explanation: Set phrases like 'generally speaking' function as sentence adverbs and need no matching subject.

questions.question_text: In "the last of the great summer festivals," the headword is —
questions.explanation: 'Last' is the head (meaning 'the last one'); 'of the great summer festivals' post-modifies it.

questions.question_text: "Visiting relatives can be boring." The sentence is ambiguous because —
questions.option_c: visiting may modify relatives or be the subject itself
questions.explanation: It can mean relatives who visit, or the act of visiting relatives — a modifier attachment ambiguity.

questions.question_text: "The chicken is ready to eat." The ambiguity arises because —
questions.option_a: to eat can be active or passive
questions.explanation: 'To eat' may mean the chicken will eat, or the chicken will be eaten.

questions.question_text: "Old men and women were invited." The adjective "old" is ambiguous because —
questions.option_d: it may modify only men or both groups
questions.explanation: We cannot tell whether the women are old too — a scope ambiguity of the pre-modifier.

questions.question_text: Which noun phrase has the correct adjective order?
questions.explanation: Correct order: opinion (beautiful), age (old), material (wooden).

questions.question_text: In "She bought three beautiful small old silver rings," the number of pre-modifiers is —
questions.explanation: 'Three, beautiful, small, old, silver' — five words modify the headword 'rings'.

questions.question_text: "Having read the instructions carefully, the machine was easy to operate." The error is —
questions.explanation: The machine did not read the instructions; the modifier lacks a human subject.

questions.question_text: "Turning the corner, the view was breathtaking." The error is —
questions.explanation: The view did not turn the corner; the participle phrase dangles.

questions.question_text: "Considering the price, the phone is excellent." The phrase "Considering the price" is —
questions.explanation: 'Considering' here functions like a preposition and is accepted without a matching subject.

questions.question_text: "Being a Sunday, the shops were closed." The error is —
questions.explanation: 'Being a Sunday' should describe a day, but the subject is 'the shops'.

questions.question_text: In "the house I live in," the post-modifier of "house" is —
questions.explanation: It is a contact (reduced) relative clause: '(that) I live in' follows the noun.

questions.question_text: In "He painted the wall green," the word "green" is —
questions.explanation: 'Green' completes the object 'wall' (the wall became green); it modifies no noun directly.

questions.question_text: In "The soup tastes strangely sweet," the word "strangely" modifies —
questions.explanation: 'Strangely' is an adverb modifying the adjective 'sweet', not the verb.

questions.question_text: "My sister, who lives in Chittagong, is a teacher." The commas show that —
questions.option_b: the speaker has only one sister
questions.option_d: who lives in Chittagong is a pre-modifier
questions.explanation: The non-restrictive clause adds extra information, which is possible only when the sister is already identified.

questions.question_text: In "He arrived safe and sound," the word "safe" is —
questions.explanation: After the linking verb 'arrived', 'safe' describes 'he'; it is not an adverb here.

questions.question_text: In "the then unknown writer," the pre-modifiers are —
questions.explanation: Both 'then' (meaning 'at that time') and 'unknown' come before the headword 'writer'.

questions.question_text: In "She passed almost every exam," the word "almost" modifies —
questions.explanation: 'Almost' sits before 'every', limiting the determiner: nearly every exam, not nearly passing.

questions.question_text: "Compared with last year, profits have doubled." The phrase "Compared with last year" is —
questions.explanation: Such introductory participles are widely accepted as sentence modifiers.

questions.question_text: Which sentence has NO modifier error?
questions.option_a: After warning about the storm, staying ashore was done.
questions.option_b: After warning about the storm, the storm kept the fishermen ashore.
questions.option_c: After warning about the storm, the fishermen stayed ashore.
questions.option_d: After being warned about the storm, the fishermen stayed ashore.
questions.explanation: Only in (b) does the participle 'being warned' correctly match the subject 'the fishermen'.

questions.question_text: In "a big old black American car," the adjective order follows —
questions.explanation: Big (size), old (age), black (colour), American (origin) follow the standard order.

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly places the modifier? "Shocked by the news, she burst into tears." vs "Shocked by the news, tears filled her eyes."
questions.explanation: 'She' was shocked, so 'she' must be the subject; tears cannot be shocked.

questions.question_text: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier? (set 2).
questions.option_c: While I was away, my plants died.
questions.option_d: My plants died while I was away.
questions.explanation: 'While away' needs a person who was away, but the subject is 'my plants'.

questions.question_text: "Having lost his key, the door remained locked." The error is —
questions.explanation: The door did not lose the key; the participle phrase needs a person as subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the best correction of "To understand the problem, the diagram must be studied."
questions.option_a: To understand the problem, you must study the diagram.
questions.option_b: To understand the problem, studying the diagram is a must.
questions.option_c: To understand the problem, the diagram must be studied by you.
questions.option_d: The diagram to understand the problem must be studied.
questions.explanation: 'You' are the one understanding, so 'you' must be the subject of the main clause.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She go to school every day.'
questions.option_a: She go to school every day.
questions.option_b: She goes to school every day.
questions.option_c: She going to school every day.
questions.option_d: She gone to school every day.
questions.explanation: Third person singular subject (she) takes verb with -s in present indefinite: goes.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'They is playing football.'
questions.explanation: Plural subject (they) takes 'are' in present continuous.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I has a pen.'
questions.explanation: First person subject (I) takes 'have', not 'has'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He don't like tea.'
questions.explanation: Third person singular takes 'doesn't' followed by base verb 'like'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is a honest girl.'
questions.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound (the h is silent), so it takes 'an'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is a best boy in the class.'
questions.option_a: He is the best boy in the class.
questions.option_b: He is a best boy in the class.
questions.option_c: He is best boy in the class.
questions.option_d: He is an best boy in the class.
questions.explanation: Superlative degree (best) takes the definite article 'the'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I saw a owl on the tree.'
questions.option_a: I saw a owl on the tree.
questions.option_b: I saw the owl on a tree.
questions.option_c: I saw an owl on the tree.
questions.option_d: I saw owl on the tree.
questions.explanation: 'Owl' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She gave me a good advice.'
questions.option_a: She gave me a good advice.
questions.option_b: She gave me a good advices.
questions.option_d: She gave me some good advice.
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'a' or a plural form; use 'some advice'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The dog bark at night.'
questions.option_d: The dog barked at night every day.
questions.explanation: Singular subject (the dog) in present indefinite takes verb with -s: barks.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'We was happy yesterday.'
questions.explanation: Plural subject (we) takes 'were' in past tense, not 'was'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He can sings well.'
questions.explanation: After a modal (can), the base form of the verb is used: sing.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She has went home.'
questions.explanation: Present perfect uses has/have + past participle: has gone.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I am agree with you.'
questions.explanation: 'Agree' is a verb, so no 'am' is needed: I agree with you.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is married with my sister.'
questions.option_a: He is married to my sister.
questions.option_b: He is married with my sister.
questions.option_c: He is married on my sister.
questions.option_d: He is married for my sister.
questions.explanation: 'Married' is followed by the preposition 'to', not 'with'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is good in English.'
questions.explanation: 'Good' takes the preposition 'at' when referring to skill in a subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He arrived to the station late.'
questions.option_a: He arrived to the station late.
questions.option_b: He arrived in the station late.
questions.option_c: He arrived at the station late.
questions.option_d: He arrived on the station late.
questions.explanation: 'Arrive at' is used for small places like a station; 'arrive to' is wrong.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I am waiting for you from morning.'
questions.option_a: I am waiting for you from morning.
questions.option_b: I have been waiting for you since morning.
questions.option_c: I am waiting for you since morning.
questions.option_d: I have been waiting for you from the morning.
questions.explanation: An action continuing from a point of time uses present perfect continuous with 'since'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'They have many luggages.'
questions.explanation: 'Luggage' is uncountable, so use 'much luggage', never 'luggages'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She bought two dozens eggs.'
questions.option_c: She bought two dozen of eggs.
questions.option_d: She bought a two dozens eggs.
questions.explanation: After a number, 'dozen' stays singular: two dozen eggs.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is more better today.'
questions.option_b: He is much better today than yesterday.
questions.explanation: Double comparatives are wrong; 'better' is already comparative, so drop 'more'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'This is the most easiest sum.'
questions.option_a: This is the most easiest sum.
questions.option_c: This is a most easiest sum.
questions.option_d: This is the more easiest sum.
questions.explanation: Double superlatives are wrong; 'easiest' is already superlative, so drop 'most'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is senior than me.'
questions.explanation: 'Senior' is followed by 'to', not 'than'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She has long hairs.'
questions.explanation: 'Hair' is uncountable when referring to the hair on the head; no plural 'hairs'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I saw him yesterday at park.'
questions.option_a: I saw him yesterday at park.
questions.option_b: I saw him yesterday in park.
questions.option_c: I saw him yesterday at the park.
questions.option_d: I saw him yesterday on park.
questions.explanation: A specific place takes the definite article: at the park.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He said me a story.'
questions.option_d: He told to me a story.
questions.explanation: 'Say' needs 'to' before an object, but 'tell' takes the object directly: told me.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She asked to him a question.'
questions.option_a: She asked to him a question.
questions.option_b: She asked for him a question.
questions.option_c: She asked him to a question.
questions.explanation: 'Ask' takes a direct object without a preposition: asked him.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'They discussed about the matter.'
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' is transitive and takes no preposition: discussed the matter.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He entered into the room.'
questions.explanation: 'Enter' takes no preposition before its object: entered the room.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She resembles to her mother.'
questions.explanation: 'Resemble' takes no preposition: resembles her mother.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He married to his childhood friend last year.'
questions.option_a: He married to his childhood friend last year.
questions.option_b: He married for his childhood friend last year.
questions.option_c: He married with his childhood friend last year.
questions.option_d: He married his childhood friend last year.
questions.explanation: 'Marry' as a verb takes a direct object with no preposition: married his childhood friend.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I know him since three years.'
questions.option_a: I have known him for three years.
questions.option_b: I know him since three years.
questions.option_c: I knew him for three years.
questions.option_d: I have known him since three years.
questions.explanation: Duration of time uses 'for', not 'since', and the tense is present perfect: have known.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is afraid from dogs.'
questions.explanation: 'Afraid' is followed by 'of', not 'from'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is angry on me.'
questions.explanation: 'Angry with' is used for a person (angry at is for a thing).

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I am interested for music.'
questions.explanation: 'Interested' takes the preposition 'in'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He knocked the door twice.'
questions.option_a: He knocked at the door twice.
questions.option_c: He knocked on the door twice loudly.
questions.option_d: He knocked to the door twice.
questions.explanation: 'Knock at the door' is the correct phrase; 'knocked on' also works but the plain form needs 'at'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She laughed on him.'
questions.explanation: 'Laugh at' is the correct phrase; 'laugh on' is wrong.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The train is more faster than the bus.'
questions.option_a: The train is more faster than the bus.
questions.option_b: The train is faster than the bus.
questions.option_c: The train is most faster than the bus.
questions.option_d: The train is more fast than the bus.
questions.explanation: 'Faster' is already comparative, so 'more' must not be added.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He runs very fastly.'
questions.explanation: 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb; 'fastly' does not exist.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She sings sweet.'
questions.explanation: A verb is modified by an adverb: sings sweetly, not the adjective 'sweet'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is too weak that he cannot walk.'
questions.option_a: He is too weak that he cannot walk.
questions.option_b: He is very weak that he cannot walk.
questions.option_c: He is so weak that he cannot walk.
questions.option_d: He is too weak so he cannot walk.
questions.explanation: The 'so...that' pattern expresses result; 'too...that' is incorrect.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I have a little friends in Dhaka.'
questions.option_a: I have a little friends in Dhaka.
questions.option_b: I have a few friends in Dhaka.
questions.option_c: I have few friend in Dhaka.
questions.option_d: I have little friends in Dhaka.
questions.explanation: 'A few' is used with countable plural nouns (friends); 'a little' is for uncountables.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'There is few water in the jug.'
questions.option_a: There is few water in the jug.
questions.option_b: There are few water in the jug.
questions.option_c: There is a few water in the jug.
questions.option_d: There is little water in the jug.
questions.explanation: 'Little' is used with uncountable nouns like water; 'few' is for countables.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is a old man.'
questions.explanation: 'Old' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She has an European friend.'
questions.explanation: 'European' begins with a consonant sound (yu), so it takes 'a'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I go to school by foot.'
questions.option_a: I go to school by foot.
questions.option_b: I go to school on foot.
questions.option_c: I go to school with foot.
questions.option_d: I go to school in foot.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'on foot', not 'by foot'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He came here by a bus.'
questions.option_a: He came here by a bus.
questions.option_b: He came here by the bus.
questions.option_c: He came here in a bus.
questions.explanation: 'By' + means of transport takes no article: by bus.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is in home now.'
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'at home', not 'in home'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He sat in the chair.'
questions.explanation: One sits 'on' a chair; 'in' is used only for armchairs in special contexts.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'They are in the bus.'
questions.explanation: For large public vehicles, the correct preposition is 'on': on the bus.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is suffering with fever.'
questions.explanation: 'Suffer from' is the correct phrase for illness.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She congratulated me for my success.'
questions.option_a: She congratulated me on my success.
questions.option_b: She congratulated me for my success.
questions.option_c: She congratulated to me for my success.
questions.option_d: She congratulated me at my success.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulate' takes the preposition 'on'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He insisted to go there.'
questions.explanation: 'Insist' is followed by 'on' + gerund: insisted on going.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I prevented him to go there.'
questions.option_a: I prevented him for go there.
questions.option_b: I prevented him from going there.
questions.option_c: I prevented him to go there.
questions.option_d: I prevented him in going there.
questions.explanation: 'Prevent' is followed by 'from' + gerund: prevented him from going.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is fond for music.'
questions.explanation: 'Fond' takes the preposition 'of'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is jealous with his friend.'
questions.option_a: He is jealous of his friend.
questions.option_b: He is jealous with his friend.
questions.option_c: He is jealous for his friend.
questions.option_d: He is jealous on his friend.
questions.explanation: 'Jealous' takes the preposition 'of'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I am tired from work.'
questions.explanation: 'Tired of' is the standard phrase for being fed up with something.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He apologized me for his mistake.'
questions.option_a: He apologized me for his mistake.
questions.option_b: He apologized to me for his mistake.
questions.option_c: He apologized for me his mistake.
questions.option_d: He apologized on me for his mistake.
questions.explanation: 'Apologize' takes 'to' before the person: apologized to me.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'They invited to me to the party.'
questions.option_a: They invited to me to the party.
questions.option_b: They invited for me to the party.
questions.option_c: They invited on me to the party.
questions.option_d: They invited me to the party.
questions.explanation: 'Invite' takes a direct object with no preposition: invited me.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He said that he is ill.'
questions.option_a: He said that he was ill.
questions.option_b: He said that he is ill.
questions.option_c: He says that he was ill.
questions.option_d: He said that he be ill.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present tense shifts to past: said... was ill.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She said me she will come.'
questions.option_a: She said to me she will come.
questions.option_b: She said me she will come.
questions.option_c: She told me she would come.
questions.option_d: She told to me she will come.
questions.explanation: Use 'told me' (no 'to') and shift 'will' to 'would' in reported speech.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Neither of the boys were present.'
questions.option_a: Neither of the boys were present.
questions.option_b: Neither of the boys was present.
questions.option_c: Neither of the boys are present.
questions.option_d: Neither of the boys have present.
questions.explanation: 'Neither of' is followed by a singular verb: was present.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Each of the students have a pen.'
questions.option_a: Each of the students have a pen.
questions.option_b: Each of the students are having a pen.
questions.option_c: Each of the student have a pen.
questions.option_d: Each of the students has a pen.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' is followed by a singular verb: has.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'One of the girls are singing.'
questions.option_a: One of the girls is singing.
questions.option_b: One of the girls are singing.
questions.option_c: One of the girl are singing.
questions.option_d: One of the girls were singing yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'One of' takes a singular verb: is singing.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The number of students are fifty.'
questions.option_a: The number of students are fifty.
questions.option_b: The numbers of students is fifty.
questions.option_c: The number of students is fifty.
questions.option_d: The number of student are fifty.
questions.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb: is.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'A number of students was absent.'
questions.option_a: A number of students is absent.
questions.option_b: A number of students were absent.
questions.option_c: A number of students was absent.
questions.option_d: A numbers of students were absent.
questions.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb: were.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The committee have decided.'
questions.explanation: A collective noun acting as a single unit takes a singular verb: has decided.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The team are playing well.'
questions.explanation: 'Team' as a single unit takes a singular verb: is playing.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Bread and butter are his breakfast.'
questions.option_a: Bread and butter are his breakfast.
questions.option_b: Bread and butter were his breakfast.
questions.option_c: Bread and butter is his breakfast.
questions.option_d: Bread and butters are his breakfast.
questions.explanation: 'Bread and butter' is a single dish, so it takes a singular verb: is.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Slow and steady win the race.'
questions.option_a: Slow and steady win the race.
questions.option_b: Slow and steady wins the race.
questions.option_c: Slow and steadies win the race.
questions.option_d: Slow and steady winning the race.
questions.explanation: 'Slow and steady' is a single idea, so it takes a singular verb: wins.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Neither he nor his brothers was there.'
questions.option_a: Neither he nor his brothers is there.
questions.option_b: Neither he nor his brother were there.
questions.option_c: Neither he nor his brothers was there.
questions.option_d: Neither he nor his brothers were there.
questions.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearest subject: brothers were.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Either Rahim or Karim are guilty.'
questions.option_a: Either Rahim or Karim is guilty.
questions.option_b: Either Rahim or Karim are guilty.
questions.option_c: Either Rahim or Karim be guilty.
questions.option_d: Either Rahim and Karim is guilty.
questions.explanation: With either...or, the verb agrees with the nearest subject: Karim is.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Not only he but also his friends was punished.'
questions.option_a: Not only he but also his friends is punished.
questions.option_b: Not only he but also his friends was punished.
questions.option_c: Not only he but also his friends were punished.
questions.option_d: Not only him but also his friends was punished.
questions.explanation: With not only...but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: friends were.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The quality of the mangoes were good.'
questions.option_a: The quality of the mangoes were good.
questions.option_b: The quality of the mangoes was good.
questions.option_c: The qualities of the mangoes were good.
questions.option_d: The quality of the mango were good.
questions.explanation: The real subject is 'quality' (singular), so the verb is singular: was.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Fifty miles are a long distance.'
questions.option_a: Fifty mile are a long distance.
questions.option_b: Fifty miles are a long distance.
questions.option_d: Fifty miles is a long distance.
questions.explanation: An amount or measurement is treated as singular: Fifty miles is.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Two-thirds of the work have been done.'
questions.option_a: Two-thirds of the work has been done.
questions.option_b: Two-thirds of the work have been done.
questions.option_c: Two-third of the work have been done.
questions.option_d: Two-thirds of the works has been done.
questions.explanation: 'Work' is uncountable, so the fraction takes a singular verb: has.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Many a man have tried.'
questions.explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and singular verb: has tried.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'More than one boy were absent.'
questions.option_a: More than one boys was absent.
questions.option_b: More than one boy was absent.
questions.option_c: More than one boy were absent.
questions.option_d: More than one boy is absent yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'More than one' takes a singular verb: was absent.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The news are good.'
questions.explanation: 'News' is singular in form and meaning, so it takes 'is'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Mathematics are difficult.'
questions.explanation: Subject names like mathematics are singular: is difficult.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The scissors is sharp.'
questions.explanation: 'Scissors' is always plural in form and takes a plural verb: are.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'If he will come, I shall go.'
questions.option_a: If he will come, I shall go.
questions.option_b: If he comes, I shall go.
questions.option_c: If he would come, I shall go.
questions.option_d: If he come, I shall go.
questions.explanation: In a first conditional, the if-clause uses present tense: If he comes.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'If I was rich, I would travel.'
questions.option_a: If I was rich, I would travel.
questions.option_b: If I were rich, I will travel.
questions.option_c: If I am rich, I would travel.
questions.option_d: If I were rich, I would travel.
questions.explanation: In an unreal second conditional, use 'were' for all persons: If I were.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Had he worked hard, he would pass.'
questions.option_a: Had he worked hard, he would have passed.
questions.option_b: Had he worked hard, he would pass.
questions.option_c: Had he work hard, he would have passed.
questions.option_d: If he had worked hard, he will pass.
questions.explanation: Third conditional needs would have + past participle: would have passed.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Unless he does not work hard, he will fail.'
questions.option_a: Unless he does not work hard, he will fail.
questions.option_b: Unless he do not work hard, he will fail.
questions.option_c: Unless he works hard, he will fail.
questions.option_d: Unless he does not works hard, he will fail.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' already carries a negative sense, so no 'not' is added.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'No sooner he came than it rained.'
questions.option_a: No sooner he came than it rained.
questions.option_b: No sooner had he come than it rained.
questions.option_c: No sooner did he came than it rained.
questions.option_d: No sooner he had come than it rained.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' takes inversion: No sooner had he come than...

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Scarcely he had reached the station when the train left.'
questions.option_a: Scarcely he had reached the station when the train left.
questions.option_b: Scarcely had he reach the station when the train left.
questions.option_c: Scarcely he reached the station when the train left.
questions.option_d: Scarcely had he reached the station when the train left.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely' takes inversion with the auxiliary before the subject.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He asked me where was I going.'
questions.option_a: He asked me where I was going.
questions.option_b: He asked me where was I going.
questions.option_c: He asked me that where I was going.
questions.option_d: He asked to me where I was going.
questions.explanation: In indirect questions, the word order is normal (subject before verb): where I was going.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She said that she can swim.'
questions.option_a: She said that she can swim.
questions.option_b: She says that she could swim.
questions.option_c: She said that she could swim.
questions.option_d: She said that she can swam.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'can' shifts to 'could'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: "He said, 'I will come tomorrow'."
questions.option_b: He said that he would come the next day.
questions.option_c: He said that he will come the next day.
questions.option_d: He said that he would come tomorrow.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, 'will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The teacher said the earth was round.'
questions.option_a: The teacher said the earth were round.
questions.option_b: The teacher said the earth was round.
questions.option_c: The teacher says the earth is round.
questions.option_d: The teacher said the earth is round.
questions.explanation: Universal truths do not change tense in reported speech: the earth is round.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He enquired me about my health.'
questions.option_a: He enquired me about my health.
questions.option_b: He enquired to me about my health.
questions.option_c: He enquired of me about my health.
questions.option_d: He enquired from me about my health.
questions.explanation: 'Enquire of' a person is the correct phrase, not 'enquire me'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Let he go there.'
questions.explanation: After 'let', the objective case is used: Let him go.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'It is me who did it.'
questions.option_a: It is me who did it.
questions.option_b: It is I who does it.
questions.option_c: It is mine who did it.
questions.option_d: It is I who did it.
questions.explanation: After 'be' in formal English, the nominative case is used: It is I.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Between you and I, he is wrong.'
questions.option_a: Between you and me, he is wrong.
questions.option_b: Between you and I, he is wrong.
questions.option_c: Between you and mine, he is wrong.
questions.option_d: Among you and me, he is wrong.
questions.explanation: A preposition takes the objective case: between you and me.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Whom did you give the book to.'
questions.option_a: Who did you give the book to?
questions.option_b: Whom you gave the book to?
questions.option_c: Whom did you give the book to?
questions.option_d: To who did you gave the book?
questions.explanation: The object of a verb in formal English takes 'whom', with normal question order.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The man which came yesterday is my uncle.'
questions.option_a: The man which came yesterday is my uncle.
questions.option_b: The man who came yesterday is my uncle.
questions.option_c: The man whose came yesterday is my uncle.
questions.option_d: The man whom came yesterday is my uncle.
questions.explanation: For people as the subject, the relative pronoun is 'who', not 'which'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'This is the house whom I bought.'
questions.option_a: This is the house whom I bought.
questions.option_b: This is the house who I bought.
questions.option_c: This is the house whose I bought.
questions.option_d: This is the house which I bought.
questions.explanation: For things, the relative pronoun is 'which', not 'whom'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: "I have read the book who's cover is red."
questions.option_a: I have read the book who's cover is red.
questions.option_b: I have read the book which cover is red.
questions.option_c: I have read the book whose cover is red.
questions.option_d: I have read the book whom cover is red.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession; 'who's' means 'who is'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She bought less books than I.'
questions.option_a: She bought less books than I.
questions.option_b: She bought less book than I.
questions.option_c: She bought fewer books than I.
questions.option_d: She bought the less books than I.
questions.explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns (books); 'less' is for uncountables.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He drank less glasses of water.'
questions.option_a: He drank less glasses of water.
questions.option_b: He drank fewer glasses of water.
questions.option_c: He drank a less glasses of water.
questions.option_d: He drank the fewer glasses of water.
questions.explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns (glasses).

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'There is less people here today.'
questions.option_a: There is less people here today.
questions.option_b: There are less people here today.
questions.option_c: There is lesser people here today.
questions.option_d: There are fewer people here today.
questions.explanation: 'People' is countable, so use 'are fewer'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is junior than me in the office.'
questions.option_a: She is junior to me in the office.
questions.option_b: She is junior than me in the office.
questions.option_c: She is junior from me in the office.
questions.option_d: She is junior over me in the office.
questions.explanation: 'Junior' is followed by 'to', not 'than'.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is my older sister.'
questions.option_d: She is my more elder sister.
questions.explanation: 'Elder' is used for members of the same family: elder sister.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'This is the most interesting of the two books.'
questions.option_a: This is the most interesting of the two books.
questions.option_b: This is the more interesting of the two books.
questions.option_c: This is a most interesting of the two books.
questions.option_d: This is more interesting of two books.
questions.explanation: For comparison between two, use the comparative degree: more interesting.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Of the two boys, Karim is the tallest.'
questions.option_a: Of the two boys, Karim is the tallest.
questions.option_b: Of the two boys, Karim is tallest.
questions.option_c: Of two boys, Karim is the taller.
questions.option_d: Of the two boys, Karim is the taller.
questions.explanation: Between two persons, the comparative is used: the taller.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is more prettier than her sister.'
questions.option_a: She is prettier than her sister.
questions.option_b: She is more prettier than her sister.
questions.option_c: She is most prettier than her sister.
questions.option_d: She is more pretty than her sister prettier.
questions.explanation: 'Prettier' is already comparative; 'more' must not be added.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Swim is a good exercise.'
questions.option_b: To swimming is a good exercise.
questions.explanation: A gerund (swimming) acts as the subject noun, not the base verb.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is addicted to smoke.'
questions.explanation: After 'addicted to', the gerund is used: addicted to smoking.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She is capable to do the work.'
questions.option_a: She is capable to do the work.
questions.option_b: She is capable for doing the work.
questions.option_c: She is capable in doing the work.
questions.option_d: She is capable of doing the work.
questions.explanation: 'Capable' takes 'of' + gerund: capable of doing.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I look forward to meet you.'
questions.option_a: I look forward to meeting you.
questions.option_b: I look forward to meet you.
questions.option_c: I look forward for meeting you.
questions.option_d: I look forwards to meet you.
questions.explanation: 'To' here is a preposition, so it takes a gerund: to meeting.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is used to get up early.'
questions.option_a: He is used to get up early.
questions.option_b: He is used for getting up early.
questions.option_c: He is used to getting up early.
questions.option_d: He used to getting up early.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' (be accustomed) takes a gerund: used to getting up.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'It is no use to cry over spilt milk.'
questions.option_a: It is no use to cry over spilt milk.
questions.option_b: It is no use crying over spilt milk.
questions.option_c: It is no uses crying over spilt milk.
questions.option_d: It is not use to cry over spilt milk.
questions.explanation: 'No use' is followed by a gerund: no use crying.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'I enjoy to read novels.'
questions.explanation: 'Enjoy' is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive: enjoy reading.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'She avoids to meet strangers.'
questions.explanation: 'Avoid' takes a gerund: avoids meeting.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He denied to steal the money.'
questions.option_a: He denied to steal the money.
questions.option_b: He denies to stealing the money.
questions.option_d: He denied for stealing the money.
questions.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by a gerund: denied stealing.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: "We are looking forward to visit Cox's Bazar."
questions.option_a: We are looking forward to visit Cox's Bazar.
questions.option_b: We are looking forward to visiting Cox's Bazar.
questions.option_c: We are look forward to visiting Cox's Bazar.
questions.option_d: We are looking forwards to visit Cox's Bazar.
questions.explanation: 'Looking forward to' takes a gerund because 'to' is a preposition here.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The doctor suggested me to take rest.'
questions.option_a: The doctor suggested me to take rest.
questions.option_b: The doctor suggested to me to take rest.
questions.option_c: The doctor suggested me taking rest.
questions.option_d: The doctor suggested that I take rest.
questions.explanation: 'Suggest' cannot take a person as object; use a that-clause: suggested that I take rest.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The box is too heavy for lift.'
questions.option_a: The box is too heavy to lift.
questions.option_b: The box is so heavy to lift.
questions.option_c: The box is too heavy that to lift.
questions.option_d: The box is very heavy to lift.
questions.explanation: 'Too...to' shows excess preventing an action: too heavy to lift.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'He is so weak to walk.'
questions.option_a: He is so weak to walk.
questions.option_b: He is very weak to walk.
questions.option_c: He is too weak to walk.
questions.option_d: He is so weak that walk.
questions.explanation: 'Too...to' is the pattern for inability: too weak to walk.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The table is to write.'
questions.option_c: The table is to be writing.
questions.explanation: Purpose of a thing is expressed with 'for' + gerund: for writing.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'The more you read, more you learn.'
questions.option_a: The more you read, more you learn.
questions.option_b: The more you read, the more you learn.
questions.option_c: More you read, the more you learn.
questions.option_d: The more you read, the most you learn.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct version of the sentence: 'Hardly he had reached home when it rained.'
